conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Virtual Meeting April 6, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Ward 3 Vacancy Process: 30-Day Charter Appointment Schedule vs. Deferral / Special Election During COVID-19
conflicts.summary: Council divided 5-2 over whether to launch an accelerated 30-day virtual appointment process to fill Vernetta Alston's Ward 3 seat under the City Charter or defer to a special election due to COVID-19 equity and access barriers.
conflicts.side_a_position: Proceed with an April 13–May 4 appointment schedule to fulfill the City Charter's mandatory language, ensure Ward 3 representation for the June budget, and avoid special-election costs.
side_a_arguments: City Charter uses mandatory 'shall' language requiring council to attempt an appointment within 60 days.
Appointing by May 4 avoids leaving Ward 3 unrepresented until December, prevents a 3-3 budget deadlock in June, and saves city funds during a fiscal crisis.
An application process can be made more accessible than self-funding and running a special-election campaign during a pandemic.
conflicts.side_b_position: Do not rush a 30-day virtual-only appointment while City Hall is closed and residents face pandemic hardships; allow more time or a special election.
side_b_arguments: Requiring virtual applications and interviews while City Hall is closed privileges residents with computers, reliable internet, and job security while excluding struggling working-class applicants.
Six members already constitute a working quorum for the budget, and overtaxed city staff should focus on COVID-19 emergency response rather than running a 30-day selection.
Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People urged allowing voters to decide via special election.
conflicts.resolution: Motion to adopt the 30-day appointment schedule passed 5-2 by roll call (later rescinded unanimously on April 20 in favor of N.C.G.S. § 160A-63).

conflicts.side_a_position: Proceed with an April 13–May 4 appointment schedule to comply with the City Charter's 'shall' mandate, seat a seventh member before the June budget vote, and avoid special-election costs.
side_a_arguments: City Charter mandates an appointment attempt within 60 days unless council deadlocks.

Six members form a full quorum for the budget, and staff capacity should remain focused on COVID-19 relief.

conflicts.resolution: Approved 5-2 by roll call (subsequently rescinded unanimously on April 20 in favor of N.C.G.S. § 160A-63).

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Feb 17, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Kendrick Estates Annexation, Stormwater Flooding Risks, and Enforceability of Developer Commitments
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 over whether to approve Baker Residential's Kendrick Estates annexation and zoning request near an adjacent park and downstream flood-prone properties, weighing city 100-year stormwater rules and housing supply against unmitigated flooding risks and non-binding annexation commitments.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve annexation and zoning because city development brings stricter 100-year stormwater treatment, adds housing supply, and incorporates park-buffer commitments.
side_a_arguments: Leaving the site unannexed in Durham County could produce a worse stormwater outcome than annexing under the city's 100-year stormwater treatment standard.

The developer addressed concerns from Durham Advocates for Sustainability, New Hope Audubon, Friends of the Park, and the Environmental Affairs Board, and agreed to reissue a commitment letter including a 5-foot fence.
Durham needs additional housing supply.
conflicts.side_b_position: Opposed moving forward due to pre-existing downstream flooding, lack of legally enforceable proffers in an annexation, and preference to await Trinity School's drainage mitigation.
side_b_arguments: Commitments made in a letter during an annexation are not legally enforceable by the city the way a rezoning development plan is.
Building should not proceed where known flooding exists without first seeing the results of Trinity School's upstream channel mitigation.
Unannexed, the parcel would yield far fewer homes on larger lots with significantly lower stormwater impact.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation ordinance, consistency statement, and zoning ordinance all passed 4-3.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Dec 16, 2019 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Annexation and 616-Unit Residential Development at 1001 Olive Branch Road (Item 14)
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 on annexing 216.241 acres at 1001 Olive Branch Road for a 616-unit single-family and townhome subdivision, debating suburban sprawl and road/climate impacts against affordable townhome supply and existing infrastructure capacity.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve annexation and rezoning to add lower-priced missing-middle townhomes and utilize already-funded city water, sewer, and fire infrastructure.
side_a_arguments: At least 30% townhomes priced in the low $200,000s (~80% AMI) meet urgent housing supply and affordability needs better than 71 large-lot homes on septic.

The city has already invested in Fire Station 17 and the Southeast Regional Lift Station anticipating growth in this corridor, and the developer committed $2M+ in road improvements, 2.5 miles of trails, and 12 preserved acres.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny annexation to prevent car-dependent suburban sprawl along a two-lane state road lacking public transit.
side_b_arguments: Adding 616 auto-oriented homes on a two-lane state road without transit undermines Durham's climate and greenhouse-gas reduction goals.
Annexing 216 greenfield acres outside the urban core strains schools, water demand, and cumulative traffic ahead of the comprehensive plan rewrite.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation passed 4-3, consistency statement passed 5-2 (Schewel voting aye), and UDO rezoning passed 6-1 (Reece voting aye, Freeman voting nay).

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council March 2, 2020 (with closed captions)
conflicts.issue: Timing of Adopting Community Safety and Wellness Task Force Bylaws Without Prior County Action
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 to adopt bylaws for the joint Community Safety and Wellness Task Force over Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton's objection that Durham County commissioners had not yet held a hearing or committed to participate.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the revised task force bylaws now to signal city commitment and invite Durham County and Durham Public Schools to join.
side_a_arguments: Bylaws already incorporated input from county, school, and court stakeholders.
Passing the bylaws puts constructive pressure on the county to act and does not preclude future amendments.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer voting on joint bylaws until Durham County has reviewed and indicated willingness to participate, and reject any moratorium on police hiring.
side_b_arguments: Passing bylaws naming the county while county commissioners are in an election cycle and have not vetted the document shows lack of inter-board courtesy.
A three-year moratorium on hiring police officers proposed in the Durham Beyond Policing document is irresponsible for a city approaching 300,000 residents.
conflicts.resolution: Motion to adopt the task force bylaws passed 6-1, with Middleton casting the sole Nay vote (Freeman voiced reservations about county buy-in during debate but voted Aye).

conflicts.issue: Non-Contiguous Annexation of 279 Townhomes at 3516 Glen Road
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 to annex 52.508 acres on Glen Road for a 279-unit townhome development, with Council Member DeDreana Freeman dissenting over incompatibility with surrounding rural homes and unequal land-conservation leverage.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the satellite annexation and townhome rezoning because it meets annexation policy, matches the Medium Density Residential FLUM, and includes strong affordability commitments.
side_a_arguments: Capping units at 1,700 heated square feet promotes natural affordability alongside $41,850 for the affordable housing fund and 25% alley-loaded design.
Developer conducted extensive community outreach and added a privacy fence proffer.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose annexing dense townhomes into a rural area of small single-family and mobile homes where residents lacked the resources to secure conservation concessions.
side_b_arguments: Dense two-story townhomes diverge sharply from neighboring rural and manufactured-home residences.
Unlike Guess Road, where affluent environmental advocates secured 30 acres of conservation, lower-income Glen Road neighbors lacked equal leverage.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation passed 6-1 (Freeman Nay); subsequent utility extension agreement, consistency statement, and PDR 7.042 zoning passed 7-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Virtual Work Session April 9, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over Durham City Council's first virtual work session on April 9, 2020, with all seven seated members present—marking Council Member Vernetta Alston's final meeting before her resignation took effect at midnight to join the North Carolina General Assembly. Council voted 7-0 to approve priority agenda additions (referring Item 4 Forest Hills Neighborhood Protection Overlay back to staff and adding supplemental Item 23 Ashton Place Development Loan Commitment), reviewed pulled consent items (including the Museum of Durham History lease, Hoover Road Park CMAR contract, VCISO cybersecurity services after the malware attack, and the Ashton Place tax-credit loan), and clarified minutes procedures. Council also voted unanimously 7-0 to authorize the City Manager to receive and expend a private foundation donation for emergent COVID-19 child-feeding and homelessness needs, and voted 7-0 to settle the April 20 regular agenda.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Farewell Tributes to Vernetta Alston, and Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel opened the council's first virtual work session, and council members offered farewell tributes to Ward 3 Council Member Vernetta Alston ahead of her midnight resignation. Council voted 7-0 to approve priority items presented by City Manager Tom Bonfield—referring Item 4 (Forest Hills NPO) back to administration, updating Item 17 (2019 Q4 Crime Report), adding supplemental Item 23 (Ashton Place Development Loan Commitment), and adding the Mayor's COVID-19 private donation item.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review and Pulled Items (Items 1, 14, 15, 21, 22, 23)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed backlog items from March 5 and new items including McDougall Terrace grant funding (Item 7) and pulled Items 1, 14, 15, 21, 22, and 23. Discussions covered Clerk minutes-summarization rules versus 'for the record' requests (Item 1), the 15-year Museum of Durham History lease with a 10-year clawback (Item 14), the Hoover Road Park soccer complex CMAR amendment (Item 15), VCISO cybersecurity recovery following the city's malware event (Item 22), and the Ashton Place affordable housing tax-credit loan commitment (Item 23).

agenda_items.title: Authorization to Accept and Expend Private Foundation COVID-19 Donation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel reported that a local private foundation sought to donate emergency funds to the city for immediate COVID-19 needs such as feeding students and seniors and homelessness support. Council members urged prioritizing rent/eviction relief for undocumented and vulnerable households alongside the countywide feeding plan, and voted 7-0 to authorize the City Manager to expend up to the amount received and report back to council.

agenda_items.title: Settle April 20 Agenda and Discuss Virtual Public Comment, Hearings, and Closed Sessions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 7-0 to settle the April 20 regular agenda (all items on consent) after noting the efficiency of reviewing 23 items virtually in about an hour. City Manager Bonfield noted budget staff would schedule an April budget session, and City Attorney Kim Rehberg advised updating council individually on a mediated legal case rather than holding a virtual closed session.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Virtual Meeting April 6, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over Durham City Council's first full virtual meeting on April 6, 2020, with all seven seated members participating. The bulk of the session featured comprehensive COVID-19 operational briefings from the Emergency Operations Center, GoDurham transit, Police Chief C.J. Davis on non-punitive Stay-at-Home enforcement, homelessness shelter-to-hotel relocation (Colin Davis), small business recovery via DurhamBusiness360.com (Andre Pettigrew), and projected FY 2020-21 sales tax and revenue losses (Bertha Johnson). Council then debated how to fill Council Member Vernetta Alston's Ward 3 seat ahead of her April 9 resignation and voted 7-0 by roll call to reluctantly accept her resignation. On a split 5-2 roll-call vote, Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Vernetta Alston, and Javiera Caballero voted Aye to adopt a 30-day Ward 3 appointment schedule (applications due April 23, appointment May 4), while DeDreana Freeman and Mark-Anthony Middleton voted Nay over pandemic equity and digital-access barriers.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Proclamations, and COVID-19 Departmental & EOC Briefings
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel opened the virtual session with proclamations for National Community Development Week and National Crime Victims' Rights Week, then led COVID-19 briefings from city leadership. Updates covered 700 teleworking employees and 911's recovery from a malware attack, GoDurham's roadway pickup zones and transit safety, Chief C.J. Davis's non-punitive Stay-at-Home enforcement and mask guidance, and EOC efforts to move medically vulnerable homeless residents from congregate shelters into hotels pending county contract approval.

agenda_items.title: COVID-19 Small Business Support and Revised Budget Outlook
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OEWD Director Andre Pettigrew presented the Small Business Advisory Coalition and new DurhamBusiness360.com portal supporting SBA CARES Act applications alongside NCWorks unemployment strain. Budget Director Bertha Johnson warned of projected 10% general fund sales tax losses (~$7.1M impact on ~$71M baseline) and up to 20% discretionary revenue declines, noting budget guidelines would be revised before the May 18 budget presentation.

agenda_items.title: Acceptance of Vernetta Alston's Resignation and Ward 3 Vacancy Replacement Process
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Procedures Committee Chair Charlie Reece proposed a 30-day schedule under the City Charter to fill Ward 3 before the June budget, adjusted after a clerk holiday check to open applications April 13, close April 23, pick finalists April 27, interview April 30, and appoint May 4. Council Member Middleton urged deferring to a November special election (citing pandemic access barriers and a resolution from the Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People), and Council Member Freeman objected to rushing a 30-day timeline; council voted 7-0 to accept Alston's resignation effective April 9 and 5-2 to adopt the 30-day schedule.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Virtual Meeting April 6, 2020 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Ward 3 Vacancy Process: 30-Day Charter Appointment Schedule vs. Deferral / Special Election During COVID-19
disagreements.summary: Council divided 5-2 over whether to launch an accelerated 30-day virtual appointment process to fill Vernetta Alston's Ward 3 seat under the City Charter or defer to a special election due to COVID-19 equity and access barriers.
disagreements.side_a_position: Proceed with an April 13–May 4 appointment schedule to fulfill the City Charter's mandatory language, ensure Ward 3 representation for the June budget, and avoid special-election costs.
side_a_arguments: City Charter uses mandatory 'shall' language requiring council to attempt an appointment within 60 days.
Appointing by May 4 avoids leaving Ward 3 unrepresented until December, prevents a 3-3 budget deadlock in June, and saves city funds during a fiscal crisis.
An application process can be made more accessible than self-funding and running a special-election campaign during a pandemic.
disagreements.side_b_position: Do not rush a 30-day virtual-only appointment while City Hall is closed and residents face pandemic hardships; allow more time or a special election.
side_b_arguments: Requiring virtual applications and interviews while City Hall is closed privileges residents with computers, reliable internet, and job security while excluding struggling working-class applicants.
Six members already constitute a working quorum for the budget, and overtaxed city staff should focus on COVID-19 emergency response rather than running a 30-day selection.
Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People urged allowing voters to decide via special election.
disagreements.resolution: Motion to adopt the 30-day appointment schedule passed 5-2 by roll call (later rescinded unanimously on April 20 in favor of N.C.G.S. § 160A-63).

meetings.title: Durham City Council March 2, 2020 (with closed captions)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel opened the March 2, 2020 City Council meeting with his State of the City address, highlighting the McDougall Terrace carbon monoxide crisis, the $95 million affordable housing bond, DEAR and Welcome Home second-chance programs, and honoring city frontline staff, 911 dispatchers, and April 10 explosion first responders. After approving the consent agenda 7-0 (excluding pulled Item 5) and voting 7-0 in two motions to add six Police Gang Unit positions (Item 17), council passed the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force bylaws (Item 22) 6-1—with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and Mark-Anthony Middleton voting Nay over acting before Durham County review. In public hearings, council unanimously approved 7-0 the 3871 Guess Road FLUM amendment and IL(D) self-storage rezoning with a 30-acre conservation easement (Item 18), and approved the 3516 Glen Road Townhomes annexation (Item 19) 6-1—with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and DeDreana Freeman voting Nay over rural character impacts—before approving the accompanying utility extension, consistency statement, and PDR 7.042 zoning 7-0. Council closed the session by approving the Urban Avenue street closing and Beltline easement agreement (Item 20) 7-0 and the $180,000 Legal Aid DEAR contract (Item 5) 7-0.

agenda_items.title: State of the City Address and Recognition of Frontline City Heroes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel delivered his 2020 State of the City address reflecting on the April 10, 2019 Brightleaf gas explosion, the relocation of 280 McDougall Terrace families, the $95 million affordable housing bond, gun violence trends, and the DEAR and Welcome Home reentry programs. He honored the Impact Team, 911 dispatcher Emily Battello, and firefighters and police officers who responded to the Brightleaf blast, followed by Jordan High School chorus music.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Item 5) and Public Comment on McDougall Terrace
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved the consent agenda 7-0 (excluding Item 5, Legal Aid of North Carolina contract, pulled for public comment). Speakers including Mr. Zayiti, Victoria Peterson, and Jackie Wagstaff criticized Durham Housing Authority leadership, asbestos concerns, and volunteer recognition regarding McDougall Terrace.

agenda_items.title: Item 17: Durham Police Department Gang Unit Staffing (Six Full-Time Positions)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers Minister Paul Scott, Mr. Zayiti, and Victoria Peterson raised concerns about criminalizing Black youth, police gang databases, and the need for economic and vocational training alongside policing. Council Member Freeman noted the Chief's program aims to offer pathways out of gangs before council voted 7-0 to authorize six full-time gang unit positions and 7-0 to recognize the associated costs.

agenda_items.title: Item 22: Community Safety and Wellness Task Force Bylaws
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Durham Beyond Policing speaker Danielle Purefoy supported expanding justice-involved and youth seats on the task force and funding non-police response research. Council Member Middleton objected to any three-year police hiring moratorium and opposed adopting bylaws before Durham County commissioners held a hearing (while Freeman also voiced concern over county buy-in), whereas Council Member Alston and Mayor Schewel argued passing the bylaws invites county action; the motion passed 6-1 with Middleton voting No.

agenda_items.title: Item 18: Public Hearing — 3871 Guess Road FLUM Amendment and Rezoning (PDR 2.00 to IL(D))
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Emily Struthers presented the request for a 10.14-acre portion of a 40-acre parcel at 3871 Guess Rd. to build a 150,000 sq. ft. two-story self-storage facility with a 30-acre permanent conservation easement and $10,000 affordable housing proffer, noting the Planning Commission recommended denial 10-2. Despite opposition over excess storage facilities, a commercial-node 'loophole,' and wetland/buffer limits, council approved the FLUM amendment, consistency statement, and UDO rezoning in three 7-0 votes.

agenda_items.title: Item 19: Public Hearing — 3516 Glen Road Townhomes Annexation, Utility Agreement, and Rezoning
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Jamie Sunyak and applicant attorney Bahati Mutisya presented a 52.508-acre non-contiguous annexation and rezoning from Rural Residential to PDR 7.042 for up to 279 townhomes capped at 1,700 heated square feet, with 25% alley-loaded units, $41,850 for the affordable housing fund, $4,500 for DPS, and a 5-foot privacy fence (Planning Commission approved 7-5). Council Member Freeman opposed annexing dense townhomes into a rural community lacking conservation advocacy (voting Nay on annexation 6-1), before council approved the utility agreement, consistency statement, and rezoning 7-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 6-1 (Annexation, Freeman Nay); Passed 7-0 (UEA, Consistency, Zoning)

agenda_items.title: Item 20: Public Hearing — Urban Avenue Street Closing and Beltline Development/Easement Agreement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Pat Young, General Services' Stacey Poston, Patrick Byker, and Braham Specialty president Mercer Stanfield presented closing 934.31 linear feet of Urban Ave. in exchange for 100 linear feet of Beltline trail construction, 15 public parking spaces, and $30,979 cash ($174,219 total value). Mayor Pro Tem Johnson and Council Members Caballero and Freeman questioned 'even trade' land swaps and surrounding Beltline gentrification before voting 7-0 to approve both the street closing and the easement agreement with JACO 949 Washington Investors LLC.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Victoria Peterson questioned why the $180,000 Legal Aid contract for the Durham Expunction and Restoration (DEAR) program did not go through an RFP and urged Legal Aid to continue representing McDougall Terrace tenants. disagreements.issue: Timing of Adopting Community Safety and Wellness Task Force Bylaws Without Prior County Action
disagreements.summary: Council voted 6-1 to adopt bylaws for the joint Community Safety and Wellness Task Force over Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton's objection that Durham County commissioners had not yet held a hearing or committed to participate.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the revised task force bylaws now to signal city commitment and invite Durham County and Durham Public Schools to join.
side_a_arguments: Bylaws already incorporated input from county, school, and court stakeholders.
Passing the bylaws puts constructive pressure on the county to act and does not preclude future amendments.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defer voting on joint bylaws until Durham County has reviewed and indicated willingness to participate, and reject any moratorium on police hiring.
side_b_arguments: Passing bylaws naming the county while county commissioners are in an election cycle and have not vetted the document shows lack of inter-board courtesy.
A three-year moratorium on hiring police officers proposed in the Durham Beyond Policing document is irresponsible for a city approaching 300,000 residents.
disagreements.resolution: Motion to adopt the task force bylaws passed 6-1, with Middleton casting the sole Nay vote (Freeman voiced reservations about county buy-in during debate but voted Aye).

disagreements.issue: Non-Contiguous Annexation of 279 Townhomes at 3516 Glen Road
disagreements.summary: Council voted 6-1 to annex 52.508 acres on Glen Road for a 279-unit townhome development, with Council Member DeDreana Freeman dissenting over incompatibility with surrounding rural homes and unequal land-conservation leverage.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the satellite annexation and townhome rezoning because it meets annexation policy, matches the Medium Density Residential FLUM, and includes strong affordability commitments.
side_a_arguments: Capping units at 1,700 heated square feet promotes natural affordability alongside $41,850 for the affordable housing fund and 25% alley-loaded design.
Developer conducted extensive community outreach and added a privacy fence proffer.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose annexing dense townhomes into a rural area of small single-family and mobile homes where residents lacked the resources to secure conservation concessions.
side_b_arguments: Dense two-story townhomes diverge sharply from neighboring rural and manufactured-home residences.
Unlike Guess Road, where affluent environmental advocates secured 30 acres of conservation, lower-income Glen Road neighbors lacked equal leverage.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation passed 6-1 (Freeman Nay); subsequent utility extension agreement, consistency statement, and PDR 7.042 zoning passed 7-0.

meetings.executive_summary: The December 2, 2019 Durham City Council session combined the biennial organizational meeting and a brief regular meeting presided over by Mayor Steve Schewel. Newly sworn members delivered remarks highlighting the 76% approval of the $95 million affordable housing bond, immigrant protection, gun violence prevention, and post-election council unity, and the council voted unanimously 7-0 to designate Jillian Johnson as Mayor Pro Tempore.
